Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Student
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Elena had been running a late-night synthesis in the graduate research wing when the ventilation system failed. The heavy, metallic tang of the aerosolized reagent filled the corridor before she realized the hazard. She remembered the sudden burn in her throat, the stinging liquid on her arms, and the frantic scramble to the decontamination showers. In the immediate aftermath, she could not articulate what had happened; the experience sat behind her teeth like a swallowed stone, untranslatable. When the fragments of that afternoon returned, they did not arrive in sequence. Sometimes she felt the burning sensation in her chest first, other times the phantom pressure against her skin, but she could never piece the timeline together into something coherent. The potency of the antiseptic smell that now permeated the campus health center made perfect sense to her, mirroring the chemical wipes used during the emergency response, while the oppressive stillness of waking in her dorm room at night mirrored the disorientation she had felt when the laboratory lights had flickered and died. Over the following weeks, Elena found herself steering clear of the science building altogether. She took longer routes across campus, rerouted her lunch breaks, and avoided the specific wing where the ventilation had failed. She had come to believe that her body kept reacting as if she were still trapped in that corridor, even when she was safely in her dorm room. Her muscles remained knotted, a permanent state of readiness that never fully released. When memories surfaced, the physical pain in her chest and shoulders returned with such precision that she would pause in the middle of a lecture, she was certain that something inside her was fundamentally broken. She tried to erase the memory of the event, pressing her palms against her temples and forcing herself to focus on mundane tasks until the sensations faded. The academic environment demanded a vigilance she could not afford. During a routine campus health visit, the sharp, antiseptic odor from the disinfectant wipes triggered a sudden tightening in her throat. She had left the waiting room before the nurse could ask her name. Similarly, nighttime in her fourth-floor apartment grew unbearable. Waking up in the dark, she would lie rigid, her heart hammering as she scanned the ceiling for any sign of a leak or a shadow. She checked the door locks twice, examined the windows, and mapped the exits of every new study room she entered, her eyes constantly scanning for structural vulnerabilities. What frightened her most was the sudden alarm she felt when someone touched her unexpectedly; a tap on the shoulder from a classmate or a light brush against her arm sent her jumping back, her breath catching as her body prepared to flee. Elena’s academic routine fractured under the weight of these responses. She stopped attending laboratory sections, substituting independent study modules that required fewer environmental cues, though the absence of peers only deepened her isolation. She could no longer trust her own body to signal safety, treating every heartbeat, every twinge of muscle, as a warning of impending exposure. She had come to believe there was something wrong with her as a person, a defect that made her unsteady in a world that required steadiness. The breaking point arrived when she found herself unable to sit through a final review session, her body locked in a continuous state of tension, her mind racing with fragments she could not name. She walked to the campus counseling center that afternoon, hoping to find a way to quiet the noise, terrified that her body would never again stop preparing her for a threat that had already passed.
